strengths: The core idea is original and interesting: repurposing TabPFN, a prior-fitted tabular transformer, as a gradient-free Q-function approximator within a Fitted Q Iteration loop, and the paper positions this clearly against ICL/meta-RL methods (RL2, Algorithm Distillation, OmniRL) and gradient-free RL (ES, KNN-TD).

The paper honestly and insightfully analyzes why the approach should not work (violations of i.i.d. assumptions, bootstrapped/self-referential targets, non-stationary visitation distributions), which is a genuine contribution to understanding ICL beyond its prior support.

The context-truncation operators (latest trajectories, naive de-duplication, embedding de-duplication, reward variance) address a real and underexplored problem for all in-context RL methods—what to do when the context budget is full—and the empirical comparison to stale-context and FIFO baselines is a useful addition.
An ablation study over the refit percentile, epsilon schedule, initial epsilon, and context budget is included, with 5 seeds per configuration.
The limitations discussion (low-dimensional dense-reward domains, sensitivity to hyperparameters, quadratic inference cost in context size, reliance on reward shaping) is candid and specific.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported: library versions, hyperparameters, reward-shaping functions, and hardware are documented in the appendix.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is too narrow to support the central claim that TabPFN-RL 'matches or surpasses' DQN. The evaluation covers only three low-dimensional classic-control tasks for 250 episodes, and in Figure 1 TabPFN-RL appears slower to learn than DQN on MountainCar-v0 and Acrobot-v0. No statistical significance tests or quantitative final-performance comparisons are reported, only qualitative reading of learning curves.

The comparison is confounded by per-environment reward shaping. The appendix reveals custom dense reward functions for every environment because TabPFN-RL 'tends not to perform well with sparse rewards.' This substantially weakens the headline claims: the method is being evaluated on reshaped, dense-reward variants of already-simple benchmarks, and the paper does not test unshaped rewards for either agent.

The claim of avoiding 'extensive hyperparameter tuning' is contradicted by the experiments: epsilon schedules and initial context sizes are set per environment (0.95/0.7/0.7 and 200/200/128), the ablation section itself states that different parameter values 'significantly impact convergence,' and reward shaping is designed per environment. This is substantial per-task tuning, comparable in effort to tuning DQN.

Only one baseline (DQN) is compared. Missing baselines such as PPO, tabular FQI with random forests/trees (the most direct non-gradient FQI comparator), or other gradient-free methods make it hard to judge whether the TabPFN prior is actually adding value over a generic non-neural FQI regressor.

Internal inconsistencies undermine credibility: the ablation reports the best context budget as 8096, while the main experiments use budgets of 128–200; the text simultaneously argues large budgets are costly due to quadratic attention. The theoretical 'contributions' are described as formalizing context-size limits, but the treatment is informal discussion rather than a theorem or quantitative bound.

The continual-learning experiments (Figure 2) appear to be single runs without seed variance reported, despite the paper's own acknowledgment of high run-to-run variance in RL; the conclusion that naive de-duplication is best rests on thin evidence.

Practical efficiency claims are questionable: the method requires 60 FQI iterations of full-context transformer inference per refit, refitting on every accepted episode, and an A100 GPU—so the 'computationally efficient' framing relative to backpropagation-based DQN is not substantiated with any wall-clock or FLOP comparison.

Engineering hacks (adding uniform noise to all rewards to avoid zero standard deviation in TabPFN's internal normalization) are disclosed but symptomatic of fitting a supervised tabular tool to RL without adaptation; the paper does not analyze when these fixes matter.

Overall significance is limited: even granting the results, the contribution establishes feasibility on toy tasks; scalability to the settings that would make gradient-free RL valuable (sparse rewards, high dimensions) is explicitly left open, so the paper is best viewed as an early exploratory workshop-style result rather than a main-track contribution.

strengths: The core idea is interesting and somewhat original: repurposing TabPFN, a meta-trained tabular ICL regressor, as a gradient-free Q-function approximator within Fitted Q Iteration is a creative and unexplored direction, and the paper situates it well against related ICL-RL work (RL2, Algorithm Distillation, OmniRL).

The discussion of prior mismatch (bootstrapped labels, non-i.i.d. transitions, shifting visitation measures violating TabPFN's i.i.d. prior) is a thoughtful and honest analysis of why the method's success is surprising, and motivates a genuinely interesting open question about the extrapolation ability of prior-fitted networks.

The paper addresses an important practical limitation of ICL-RL methods—what to do when the context is full—proposes several truncation operators (L, ND, ED, RV), and evaluates them against sensible baselines (stale context, latest transitions).
The limitations section is candid: it acknowledges the low-dimensional dense-reward setting, quadratic inference cost, hyperparameter sensitivity, and reliance on reward shaping.
weaknesses: The central claim of the abstract that the method works 'without any gradient descent or any extensive hyperparameter tuning' is contradicted by the paper's own evidence: the appendix reveals per-environment ε values (0.95, 0.7, 0.7), per-environment context sizes (200, 200, 128), different ε decays (0.9955, 0.99, 0.99), and per-environment hand-crafted reward shaping functions. The ablation study further states that 'different parameter values significantly impact the model's convergence,' directly undermining the motivating claim that gradient-free RL reduces hyperparameter sensitivity.

The evaluation is too limited to support the framing. Only three toy classic-control environments with low-dimensional states are tested, and even these require environment-specific reward shaping because the method 'tends not to perform well with sparse rewards.' Claims about gradient-free RL being preferable in 'sparse, non-smooth, or highly stochastic environments' (Introduction) are therefore untested—the method demonstrably fails in exactly the sparse-reward regime.

The comparison to DQN is not convincing. Both methods are run on shaped rewards (non-standard for these benchmarks), results are shown as single learning-curve plots without statistical significance testing, and there is no wall-clock or compute comparison despite claims of computational efficiency—while the paper itself concedes that quadratic inference cost 'can outweigh the savings from omitting back-propagation.'

The 'theoretical' contributions are informal. The sections on prior mismatch and context-size limits are qualitative discussions, not theorems or propositions; the formalization promised in the abstract ('We further formalize the intrinsic context size limit') amounts to the trivial observation that an ICL model with budget B stops learning when the context is full.

The context-truncation study is thin: evaluated on one environment with 5 seeds, and the reported outcome (ND beats L 'in the long run') is based on visual inspection of noisy curves; the ED and RV methods 'seem to fail as the episodes progress' without explanation or analysis.

There are presentation and correctness concerns: the description of TabPFN-FQI says TabPFN 'predicts the Bellman targets,' when in fact it is fit to regress onto them; the context-size ablation text says 'multiples of two,8' and 'a size of 8096' (inconsistent with 8192); Figure 2/3 descriptions are hard to reconcile with the text; the trivial reward-noise perturbation hack (U(0, 10^-4)) to work around TabPFN's internal normalization is a sign of fragile adaptation.

Reproducibility is partial: hyperparameters are listed, but no code release is mentioned, and the authors state they 'cannot guarantee that these are the optimal results,' making the reported DQN comparison dependent on a possibly suboptimal baseline configuration.

strengths: Novel and interesting idea: repurposing TabPFN, a prior-fitted network trained purely on synthetic i.i.d. tabular tasks, as a gradient-free Q-function approximator via FQI is a creative recombination that has not, to the authors' knowledge, been explored before.

The paper honestly identifies and analyzes the fundamental prior mismatch between TabPFN's i.i.d. assumptions and the bootstrapped, non-stationary targets/distributions of RL; this discussion is thoughtful and frames an interesting open question about the generalization capacity of ICL beyond prior support.

The continual learning problem when the ICL context is full is genuinely underexplored for ICL-based RL, and the proposed truncation operators (L, ND, ED, RV) with baselines (stale context, latest-B) constitute a useful empirical contribution.

An ablation study over percentile refit, epsilon schedule, initial epsilon, and context budget is provided, with multiple seeds (5 per ablation setting), and the appendix gives reasonably detailed implementation and reward-shaping formulas.

The limitations discussion is candid: low-dimensional dense-reward domains only, sensitivity to hyperparameters, quadratic inference cost in context size, and reliance on reward shaping are all acknowledged by the authors.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim ('TabPFN-RL matches or surpasses DQN') rests on only three low-dimensional classic-control environments over 250 episodes, with no statistical significance testing reported; the figures rely on visual comparison of noisy learning curves with shaded bands, which does not robustly support 'matches or surpasses'.

Reward shaping is a serious confound: the authors admit TabPFN-RL fails on the original sparse rewards and apply environment-specific dense shaping functions. The paper does not clearly establish whether DQN receives identical shaping, and solving these environments essentially reduces to the shaping design, weakening claims about the method itself.

The computational-efficiency motivation is not substantiated: no wall-clock time, FLOPs, or inference-cost comparison against DQN is reported, despite the authors noting quadratic attention cost per step with refitting after every accepted episode. Claims of 'fast and computationally efficient RL' are unsupported and likely unfavorable.

There is an apparent inconsistency between the ablation (best context size 8096) and the main experiments (context sizes 200, 200, 128), and the appendix admits final hyperparameters are not guaranteed optimal and differ per environment (epsilon 0.95, 0.7, 0.7), undermining the 'no extensive hyperparameter tuning' claim in the abstract.

Only one baseline (DQN) is compared; missing comparisons to PPO, simple tabular/KNN Q-learning, or even a random/linear baseline, and no comparison to other ICL-RL methods (RL2, Algorithm Distillation, OmniRL) despite them being the closest related work.

The theoretical contributions are informal: the 'formalization' of the context-size limit is essentially the observation that learning stops when the context is full, and the prior-mismatch analysis, while insightful, is qualitative with no theorems, guarantees, or quantified analysis.

The truncation-operator results are mixed and fragile: only naive de-duplication (ND) remains effective long-term while ED and RV 'seem to fail as the episodes progress', and this is evaluated in only one environment regime, so the continual-learning contribution is narrower than suggested.

No code release is mentioned, and details such as how FQI regression is run over TabPFN's discrete-bucket outputs for Q-values and how actions are selected during FQI iterations are underspecified, hurting reproducibility.

Internal inconsistencies suggest insufficient polish: e.g., a stray '8' in the ablation text, inconsistent naming (DN/DE in future work vs. ND/ED in methods), and the Acrobot-shaped reward stated without connecting it to the original sparse-reward termination condition.

strengths: The core idea is interesting and well-motivated: reusing a general-purpose in-context regression foundation model (TabPFN) as a Q-function approximator via Fitted Q-Iteration, requiring no RL-specific pretraining and no gradient updates at the RL stage. This is a clean reduction (RL -> ICR) and a genuinely different point in the design space compared to meta-trained in-context RL agents (RL^2, Algorithm Distillation, OmniRL).

The Discussion (Section 5) honestly identifies the prior-data mismatch problem (i.i.d. pretraining vs. correlated, non-stationary, bootstrapped targets), and the Limitations section candidly admits sparse-reward struggles, untested high-dimensional scaling, and quadratic runtime — a well-calibrated self-assessment.

The context-engineering study (Section 4.1, Figures 3-5) is a useful empirical contribution: deduplication-based context management enables continued learning under a fixed context budget and reduces runtime, a question relevant to any in-context RL method.

The paper reports ablations (Appendix C) including exploration schedules, context size, and FQI iteration counts, and includes additional backbone comparisons (TabICL, TabFlex, KNN in Appendix D), which supports the claim that the framework is backbone-agnostic.
Implementation details are relatively thorough (baselines, hyperparameters, seeds, hardware), aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim ('competitive with DQN, PPO, and TRPO') is overstated relative to the evidence. On Acrobot-v1 (Figure 2, bottom), DQN clearly outperforms ICR-RL (~ -100 vs ~ -120 at episode 250), and on CartPole and MountainCar the advantage over DQN is modest and within large variance bands. There are no statistical significance tests despite 10 seeds, and the conclusions/abstract assert 'matches or exceeds' without qualification.

All main results rely on environment-specific dense reward shaping (Appendix B.2), applied because the method 'tends not to perform well with sparse rewards.' While baselines reportedly use the same shaped rewards, this substantially changes the problem difficulty (e.g., dense-reward MountainCar is a much easier exploration problem) and narrows the scope of the claim to dense-reward, low-dimensional classic control. The paper admits this, but the abstract and conclusions do not reflect this limitation.

The 'zero-shot' and 'no hyperparameter tuning' framing is misleading. Table 1 claims Zero-Shot = check for ICR-RL, yet the method requires per-environment reward shaping, environment-specific epsilon schedules (epsilon_0 = 0.95 vs 0.7), environment-specific decay rates, tuned percentile-refit gates, tuned alpha, and context budget B. Ablations (Figures 7-9) show convergence depends heavily on these choices, contradicting the narrative that ICR-RL avoids the hyperparameter burden of gradient-based RL.

The alpha ablation result (Figure 8) shows performance degrading as alpha increases, 'in stark contrast to the FQI theory,' yet the paper offers no analysis of why its theoretical grounding (FQI convergence) fails in practice. This undercuts the paper's own theoretical framing (Sections 2 and 4): if the empirical behavior contradicts the FQI contraction argument, the claimed connection needs explanation, not just the label 'surprising.'

Evaluation scale is very limited: three classic-control Gymnasium environments with 2-6 dimensional state spaces and discrete actions, 250 episodes. Given the paper's ambition ('proof-of-concept for a new paradigm in RL'), at least one moderately harder or continuous-action environment would be expected for a main-track contribution.

Presentation issues: Figure 2's caption lists both PPO and TRPO as 'blue' (one is mislabeled); Figure 3 lacks axis/legend clarity about which curve is which beyond the caption; Table 1's comparison rows are qualitative checkboxes that arguably flatter the method (e.g., 'zero-shot' as discussed above). The K = alpha/(1-gamma) iteration rule is stated without derivation or justification.

The contribution sits close to prior work: FQI with an arbitrary regressor is standard, and swapping in TabPFN is a fairly direct substitution; the novelty rests mainly on the empirical surprise that an off-the-shelf ICR FM tolerates the non-i.i.d. FQI targets. Given the small evaluation and the unresolved tension with FQI theory (alpha ablation), this surprise is documented but not explained, limiting the conceptual advance.

No mention of code release, and wall-clock comparisons to gradient baselines are only reported as normalized runtime among ICR-RL variants (Figure 5), not versus DQN/PPO/TRPO, so the practical cost of per-step transformer inference (a query batch over all actions at every environment step) is not transparently quantified.

strengths: The core idea — reducing RL to in-context regression by using a pre-trained regression foundation model (TabPFN) as the function approximator inside Fitted Q-Iteration — is a clean and interesting conceptual reduction, and the paper is explicit in framing it as a proof-of-concept.
The method is genuinely gradient-free at the RL level, and the iterative ICR-FQI inference procedure is clearly described and easy to follow (Algorithm 1, Figure 1).

The context-engineering study (Section 4.1, Figures 3-5) addresses a real and under-explored practical problem for in-context RL agents (what to do when the context budget is full), and includes sensible baselines (stale context, latest episodes).
Implementation details are relatively thorough (Appendix B covers seeds, hyperparameters, baseline configurations, and even a necessary numerical hack of adding uniform reward noise).
The paper is honest in its limitations section about sparse rewards, untested high-dimensional scaling, and quadratic runtime, and the discussion of the prior-data mismatch (Section 5) is thoughtful.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are not supported at the required strength. The abstract and introduction claim ICR-RL is 'competitive with' DQN, PPO, and TRPO, but Figure 2 shows DQN clearly outperforming ICR-RL on Acrobot, and comparisons rely on only three classic-control environments with reward shaping applied to all methods — the shaped dense-reward tasks are no longer the standard benchmarks, which weakens the external validity of the comparison.

There is a significant gap between the framing and the evidence. Table 1 and the text tout 'zero-shot generalization to unseen environments' and 'continuous state-action support' as unique properties, yet no experiment demonstrates zero-shot transfer, and all evaluated environments have discrete action spaces. These properties are asserted, not demonstrated.

The method is not actually as 'training-free' as advertised: it involves per-environment online data collection, iterative ICR-FQI refitting, environment-specific reward shaping, environment-specific epsilon schedules (epsilon_0=0.95 vs 0.7), and hyperparameters tuned per environment (Appendix B, Figure 9). The claimed advantage over 'brittle' gradient methods is undermined by the ablations showing strong sensitivity to epsilon scheduling, context budget, and the number of iterations.

The ablation result that fewer FQI iterations (alpha=0.1) dramatically outperforms the theoretically motivated regime is presented as 'in stark contrast to FQI theory' but is not analyzed or explained; this unexplained deviation from theory is a red flag for the mechanistic understanding of why the method works at all.

Missing computational comparison with baselines: Figures 4-5 only compare runtime among the context-engineering variants, normalized internally. Without wall-clock comparison to DQN/PPO/TRPO, the practical cost of many forward passes through TabPFN per action selection and per FQI iteration is unknown.

Presentation and citation quality issues: Figure 2's caption lists 'DQN (blue)' and 'TRPO (blue)' for two different colors; Figure 4/7 uses '8096' versus '8192' for the context size; references [32] and [33] are exact duplicates; reference [19] (TabICLv2, arXiv 2602.11139, dated 2026) and [21] (NeurIPS vol. 38, 2026) appear to be fabricated or erroneous citations. These errors collectively suggest insufficient care.

The reward-noise perturbation (Appendix B: adding U(0,1e-4) noise to rewards to avoid division by zero in TabPFN's z-score normalization) and the need for reward shaping reveal that the method only functions after non-trivial task-specific massaging, which is not reflected in the headline narrative of an 'out of the box' foundation-model RL agent.

No code release is mentioned, and given the many implementation-specific details (context gating quantile, epsilon scheduling phases, noise injection), reproducibility without released code is doubtful.

strengths: The core idea is genuinely interesting: reducing RL to in-context regression and reusing an off-the-shelf regression FM (TabPFN) that has never seen MDP data is a surprising and conceptually valuable demonstration, complementing prior in-context RL methods (RL^2, Algorithm Distillation, OmniRL) that all require RL-specific meta-training.

The context-engineering study (Section 4.1, Figure 3) addresses a real problem for in-context RL — what to do when the context budget fills — and the de-duplication methods are a reasonable, reproducible set of heuristics with supporting runtime/memory analyses (Figures 4-5).

The paper is generally well-organized, with a clear ICR-FQI/ICR-RL decomposition, an honest limitations section (sparse rewards, quadratic runtime, untested high-dimensional scaling), and a thoughtful discussion of the TabPFN prior-data mismatch.

The ablations (Figures 7-9) are reasonably thorough, with multiple seeds per setting, and the finding that fewer FQI iterations than theory suggests works better (Figure 8) is an interesting empirical observation.
Implementation details for the method and all baselines are provided (Appendix B), and additional baselines (KNN, TabICL, TabFlex) are included in Appendix D.
weaknesses: The evaluation scope is very narrow: only three low-dimensional classic-control environments for 250 episodes. For a paper whose central claim is that ICR foundation models can 'effectively solve RL tasks' and serve as 'a foundation for RL-oriented models,' this is far from sufficient evidence; no Atari, MiniGrid, MuJoCo, or even a fourth environment is tested.

The evaluation relies on custom dense reward shaping for all three environments (Appendix B.2) because the method 'tends not to perform well with sparse rewards.' This changes the task and weakens the main results substantially; the sparse-reward comparison (Figure 6) actually shows the primary backbone (TabPFN) performing poorly, and the remedy is swapping in a different FM — which undercuts the generality narrative.

Several headline claims are unsupported: Table 1 and the text claim 'zero-shot generalization to unseen environments' and 'generalizes to completely OOD environments,' but no zero-shot or OOD transfer experiment appears anywhere — ICR-RL performs iterative FQI refitting with environment interaction, which is not zero-shot in the sense of OmniRL or RL^2. These comparative claims in Table 1 should be revised or backed by experiments.

The framing that gradient-based RL is overly brittle and hyperparameter-sensitive while ICR-RL avoids this is contradicted by the paper's own evidence: the ablations show that epsilon schedule, alpha, context budget B, and the add-gate quantile all significantly affect convergence, and the method requires non-obvious hacks (e.g., injecting uniform reward noise to avoid division by zero in TabPFN's z-score normalization, a 0.95-quantile return gate). A systematic hyperparameter scan was still needed.

Baseline comparisons are potentially unfair or at least not controlled: with dense shaped rewards, all methods should trivially improve, yet DQN still clearly outperforms ICR-RL on Acrobot-v1 and matches it on CartPole. There are no significance tests, no wall-clock/compute comparison to baselines (the quadratic-complexity runtime of TabPFN inference is a serious practical cost), and mixed results are summarized as 'competitive.'

Presentation and citation hygiene issues: Figure 2's caption lists both DQN and TRPO as blue; '8096' appears instead of 8192 in Figure 7; Figure 4/9 context budgets are inconsistent with the stated 'multiples of 8'; references [32] and [33] are duplicates; and several references are dated 2026 (including NeurIPS volume 38) with a 2026 arXiv identifier, which casts doubt on citation accuracy.

The theoretical framing is thin: the convergence argument hand-waves 'under proper data coverage assumptions' to cite FQI theory, but TabPFN violates the i.i.d./stationary regression assumptions (as the Discussion itself concedes), so no actual guarantee applies to ICR-FQI.
